incumbent_fragility: NBER: private grad lending collapsed after Grad PLUS expanded in 2006 and never recovered; capital constraints; legal limits on using program-level outcomes data in underwriting; fields with flat earnings gradients (social work, counseling, PT) cannot carry private loans; incumbents are credit-conservative.
funded_startups_already_here: GradBridge ($20M Series A, Acorn/Oaktree; second-look lending; date conflicts Oct 2025 vs Jun 2026). Climb ($50M Goldman UIG, 2019). Prodigy Finance (international-student lending, 2017). Searches for Juno, Mos, Stride, Edly returned nothing (not proof they don't exist).
wedge_hints: School-sponsored or risk-shared lending in law/MBA and other steep-earnings programs (NBER notes institutions emerging as intermediaries); warehouse/ABS capital plumbing for new originators; programs just outside the 'professional' $50k cap; outcomes-based underwriting that survives fair-lending review.
insider_roles: Grad-school financial aid directors; law/medical school CFOs and enrollment deans; consumer-lending credit-risk heads; ABS structurers; fair-lending counsel.

name: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
size_basis: EdChoice 2026 Spending Share Rankings: private school choice programs allocated $10.6B in the latest year, +29% from $8.2B. Florida $3.7B, Arizona $1.06B (prior-year ranking). Texas TEFA ESA ($1B initial, up to ~90,000 accounts, run by contractor Odyssey) began paying Jul 1, 2026. Federal credit from Jan 1, 2027: $1,700/taxpayer; Education Reform Now (cited by Third Way) estimates $1.6B/yr at 2% participation to $8B at 10%. SGOs must spend >=90% of income on scholarships, so operator take is thin (3-5% of $10.6B = $300-500M sector-wide).
money_flow: States (and from 2027 donors via SGOs) fund family accounts or vouchers; families spend on private-school tuition, homeschool vendors, tutors and therapists; a platform vendor runs applications, payments and audits for a fee.
shock: Federal tax-credit scholarship enacted in the July 2025 reconciliation law; Treasury/IRS opt-in notice Dec 12, 2025; program launches Jan 1, 2027; IRS announced 27 states opted in as of Jun 8, 2026. Texas $1B ESA launched Jul 2026. Arizona treasurer issued a June 2026 RFI to replace/upgrade its ESA platform with fraud detection after the Auditor General found as few as 6.5% of purchases audited.
incumbents: ClassWallet (Arizona and other states; ~$102.6M raised incl. $95M growth round Mar 2023), Odyssey (Texas turnkey ESA admin), state education agencies/treasuries, nonprofit SGOs.
incumbent_fragility: Vendors are being audited and re-bid (Arizona). ECCA SGO infrastructure does not exist at scale; Treasury rules not final, including whether the 90% test covers all income and how the 300%-of-area-median income eligibility is verified.
funded_startups_already_here: ClassWallet (Guidepost Growth Equity-led $95M, Mar 2023; ~$102.6M total per CB Insights); Odyssey ($10M Series A led by Tusk Venture Partners). No other funded ESA/SGO platforms found.
wedge_hints: Risk-based audit/fraud analytics for state treasuries; ECCA SGO operating platform (donor portal, income-eligibility checks, 90% accounting, state-list compliance) for the many new SGOs; microschool/small-private-school back office that bills ESAs; provider onboarding for ESA-eligible therapists and tutors.
insider_roles: State ESA program directors; treasury/comptroller staff; SGO executive directors; private-school business managers; microschool founders; state auditor staff.

name: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
size_basis: My derivation: MHI April 2026 report (read): seasonally adjusted annual shipments 103,703; YTD through April 33,054 (-7.3%); 57.7% multi-section. Census prices (secondary): new single-section ~$88-91k, double-section ~$161-164k, excluding land, delivery and setup. Blended ~$131k x ~104k homes = ~$13.6B. FHFA says chattel loans are 70-80% of new manufactured homes, so ~$9-11B chattel originations. Lot rent is a separate stream (MHI: >43,000 communities, ~4.3M homesites), not included.
money_flow: Buyers pay manufacturers, retail dealers and installers; most finance with chattel loans from specialized lenders; many homes sit on leased lots paying lot rent. Signers: buyer via dealer; dealer principal for lender partnerships; chattel lender CEO for servicing/securitization.
shock: June 2026 rule proposals: FHFA proposed replacing Duty to Serve with an outcome framework emphasizing chattel loans (91 FR 37848, published June 24, 2026; final expected effective by Jan 1, 2028); HUD proposed June 12, 2026 to require the permanent chassis only for lowest-floor sections, enabling multistory homes (HUD est. $4,800-6,700 saved per multistory unit; comment closed Aug 11, 2026; not final). ICBA opposes GSE expansion under conservatorship.
incumbents: Clayton (Berkshire; 21st Mortgage, Vanderbilt), Cavco, Skyline Champion (names from background knowledge, not re-verified); chattel lenders; community owners including private equity (Florida, Michigan, Texas heavy).
incumbent_fragility: GSEs do not buy chattel loans, so lenders charge high rates and portfolio their loans; a GSE chattel channel would reprice the market. Lot-rent disputes and state bills pressure community owners.
funded_startups_already_here: Zippy (digital chattel lender, $26M total, last reported July 2023); CoverTree (manufactured-home insurance, $13M Series A May 2024); Tammac Holdings ($60M debt and equity, undated); Apollo manufactured-housing fund ($850M first close late 2025, institutional not a startup). Few venture-funded players found.
wedge_hints: Chattel origination and servicing platform built to GSE standards so loans become securitizable; conversion finance for resident-owned communities; land-lease home insurance and escrow; dealer-side finance workflow.
insider_roles: Manufactured-home retail dealership managers, chattel underwriters and servicers, community operators, state manufactured housing association executives, plant managers, installers.

name: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
size_basis: GBP 10B repairs and maintenance in the year to 31 March 2025 for private registered providers (GBP 3.9B capitalised), up 13% from GBP 8.8B; forecast average GBP 10.9B a year over five years; at 1.30 USD per GBP. Excludes council housing repairs, so the true pool is larger.
money_flow: Tenant rents, grants and borrowing pay landlords, who pay contractors (Mears, Wates, Kier and similar, from memory) and in-house repair teams, who pay trades.
shock: Awaab's Law phase 1 took effect 27 October 2025: emergency hazards within 24 hours and short deadlines to investigate and make safe damp and mould; more hazards added in 2026 and 2027. The government impact assessment shows only GBP 10.8M a year net cost to business, which the sector and an acknowledging official say vastly understates cost.
incumbents: Large repair contractors and housing-management software vendors (NEC, MRI, Civica, from memory). Nineteen providers with 40,000+ homes hold 42% of units and 47% of turnover.
incumbent_fragility: Schedule-of-rates contracts pay per job rather than per outcome; legacy systems cannot track new legal clocks; landlord margins are already stretched by rent caps.
funded_startups_already_here: Switchee (Mould iQ launched May 2025 with three housing associations covering 92,000 homes), Mobysoft (RepairSense and a damp-and-mould module), Aico (HomeLINK sensors), Made Tech. Funding amounts not found.
wedge_hints: Compliance clock and Ombudsman-ready evidence trail for Awaab's Law cases; dispatch of sub-GBP 500 hazard jobs across small subcontractors; ventilation and mould-remediation crews as a service; contractor performance audit for landlords.
insider_roles: Repairs managers and damp-and-mould leads at housing associations, contractor operations directors, Housing Ombudsman case officers, surveyors.

name: Japan shippers' spend on contracted road freight (multi-tier trucking subcontract chain)
size_basis: Derived: about 63,000 truck operators (MLIT, undated) x JPY 264M average 2023 revenue (All Japan Trucking Association management analysis) = about JPY 16.6T (about $110B at 150 JPY per USD). Whole logistics market about JPY 24.2T for FY2023 per a secondary summary of MLIT data. 99.5% of operators have capital of JPY 300M or less.
money_flow: Shippers pay prime carriers and forwarders, who sub-contract down multi-tier chains of small carriers.
shock: On 1 Jan 2026 the Subcontract Act became the Act on Proper Transactions for SME Entrusted Businesses, widening coverage to companies above 300 staff; Trucking Business Act amendments require written contracts itemizing charges (including fuel surcharges) and an actual-carrier register; designated shippers must appoint a Chief Logistics Officer and file a first medium- to long-term plan by end of October 2026.
incumbents: Yamato, Sagawa, NX, Fukuyama (from memory), over 60,000 small carriers, and forwarders earning layered intermediary margins.
incumbent_fragility: The new laws attack intermediary margin and unpaid waiting time; small carriers lack compliance capacity; the driver overtime cap (the 2024 problem) shrinks capacity.
funded_startups_already_here: Hacobu (MOVO; JPY 700M in May 2025, cumulative above JPY 5.6B), T2 (autonomous trucking; JPY 5B pre-Series B Aug 2025, JPY 16.5B-plus cumulative per one July 2026 report). CBcloud not verified.
wedge_hints: Compliance back-office for about 60,000 small carriers (contracts, itemized charges, registers); waiting-time and berth data for shippers' CLO plans due October 2026; accessorial-charge billing and collection.
insider_roles: Transport managers (unko kanrisha), dispatchers at mid-size carriers, forwarder pricing staff, warehouse berth managers, JFTC and MLIT enforcement officers.

name: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
size_basis: Outstanding gold loans ~INR18.6 lakh crore in Mar 2026 (Experian/CRIF bureau data, +50% y/y), ~INR20 lakh crore by Sept 2026 (RBI governor sees no overheating) = ~$200-215B; blended yield ~10% (conservative; NBFC rates far higher than bank rates, 13% blend gives ~$26B) = ~$20B/yr interest. Figures conflict by definition: RBI bank-only series was only ~INR4 trillion ($43B) in Jan 2026. Mostly search-summarized, not fetched.
money_flow: Borrowers (farmers, shopkeepers, small traders, households pledging family jewellery) pay interest and fees to banks and NBFCs (Muthoot, Manappuram, IIFL, SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Federal, South Indian) and informal pawnbrokers/jewellers; lenders vault the gold, value it with in-house appraisers and auction on default.
shock: RBI 'Lending against Gold and Silver Collateral Directions, 2025' (notified 6 Jun 2025) had to be adopted by 1 Apr 2026: LTV caps 85% (to INR2.5 lakh) / 80% (to INR5 lakh) / 75% above, LTV must hold through tenor; bullet consumption loans capped at 12 months; gold handled at lender's own branches by own employees with secure facility; assaying/purity standards; formal auction SOP with empanelled auctioneers; INR5,000/day compensation for late release. Plus a gold price run-up (one outlet: peak ~$5,595/oz on 29 Jan 2026, then ~27% fall; single commentator, unverified) and NBFC share of retail gold loans rising from 28% to 40% in a year.
incumbents: Muthoot Finance (market cap crossed INR1 trillion in Jun 2025), Manappuram (Bain Capital approved to take up to ~41.7%), IIFL, plus banks (SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Federal, South Indian) and informal pawnbrokers. They earn on branch networks, local trust, vaults and high NBFC yields.
incumbent_fragility: Incumbents are strong, not fragile. The fragility is in the manual process underneath: staff appraisal, physical vaults, paper auctions, fake/under-carat gold fraud, and a thin price buffer if gold falls (one commentator says 7-8%). The own-branch/own-employee rule blocks doorstep and outsourced sourcing models, so incumbents' physical networks become a moat and startups must serve lenders rather than compete with them.
funded_startups_already_here: Rupeek (Peak XV-backed, >$164M raised; 2024 down round at ~INR1,785 crore valuation; profit after tax INR15 crore in H1 of the current FY; reportedly seeking $50M in 2026; works with Federal Bank, South Indian Bank, Axis; co-lending with Indian Bank). IndiaGold could not be verified. No 2025-26 closed rounds confirmed. Search summaries only.
wedge_hints: (1) NPA/auction disposal marketplace built to the new RBI auction SOP. name: US personal-auto physical-damage claims (collision + comprehensive): insurer payments for repair, parts, calibration and total-loss payouts
size_basis: NAIC data via trade press: private-passenger physical-damage premiums about $154.3B in 2024 at a 59.9% loss ratio, so about $92B incurred losses (my arithmetic). Includes comprehensive, glass and theft, so the collision-shop revenue slice is smaller and not sized. NAIC report itself not opened.
money_flow: Drivers pay premiums to insurers. Insurers pay repair shops (labor, paint, parts, ADAS calibrations), parts distributors and OEMs, and cash out total losses to owners. Estimating and valuation platforms (CCC, Mitchell/Enlyte, Solera) take per-claim fees.
shock: 25% Section 232 tariff on non-USMCA auto parts effective May 3, 2025. CCC Crash Course 2026 (Mar 31, 2026, covering 2025): record 23.1% total-loss frequency, calibrations on 28.3% of repairable estimates (up from 21.8%), 72% of total-loss valuations on vehicles 7+ years old. Secondary: average repair cost $4,818, repairable claim volume -9.7%. Parts prices +3.8% and repair/maintenance +5% y/y in Apr 2026 (Scripps). NOTE: the widely repeated $3.4B / 2.7% tariff figure is a 2018 PCI projection, not current. An S&P headline claims a one-time $12B+ private-auto tariff hit (page not opened, unverified).
incumbents: CCC Intelligent Solutions (public), Mitchell/Enlyte and Solera/Audatex own estimating, valuation and workflow. Insurers steer volume via direct-repair programs. Large MSOs (Crash Champions, Caliber, Gerber) are consolidating; Crash Champions renewed with CCC and expanded AI estimating in Aug 2026.
incumbent_fragility: Insurer and shop are adversaries paying the same platform vendor, so neither can fix the other's incentives. Total-loss valuation (23.1% of claims) is the one step where the policyholder has no advocate. Each new calibration is a line item nobody in the chain owns. Tariff pass-through is slow and uneven across parts, and shops are squeezed between insurer-set labor rates and rising parts cost.
funded_startups_already_here: Revv ($20M Series A, about late 2024; AI inspections and supplier links for independent shops; lead investor conflicts between sources), ServiceUp ($55M Series B led by PeakSpan, Jul 2025; $70M total; fleet and insurance repair management), Tractable ($65M Series E, 2023; AI damage estimating), VaraFix (AI estimate review launched Aug 25, 2026; no funding disclosed), CrashBay ($1.25M, Apr 2024). Nothing funded found on ADAS-calibration networks or policyholder-side total-loss audit.
wedge_hints: (1) ADAS calibration capacity and scheduling for shops. (2) Tariff-aware parts sourcing and price-lock for independent shops (PartsTrader is the incumbent to check). (3) Missed-operations and supplement audit for shops. (4) Policyholder-side total-loss valuation audit on contingency; check state total-loss rules and public-adjuster licensing. $100M revenue is about 0.11% of loss dollars, so a thin per-claim take works if one channel (large MSO or carrier program) is won.
insider_roles: Collision shop estimators and owners, DRP managers at carriers, total-loss adjusters, ADAS calibration technicians, parts managers, public adjusters, auto-claims litigators.

name: US businesses' spend on uniform, linen and workwear rental (incl. healthcare linen)
size_basis: TRSA/Oxford Economics industry economic output $27.7B in 2024 (304,000 jobs). Narrower First Research definition ~$14B. Bottom-up: Cintas Uniform Rental and Facility Services $8.62B (FY2026), Vestis ~$2.6-2.7B (quarterly ~$660M), UniFirst ~$2.4B (from memory, unverified); top 3 ~$13.7B before Alsco, Elis, healthcare linen and regional laundries.
money_flow: About 1.5M US businesses (restaurants, auto shops, hospitals, factories, hotels) pay route-based rental companies weekly/monthly for uniforms, mats, towels, linen, restroom and first-aid supplies under 3-5 year evergreen contracts with loss/damage charges and annual price escalators.
shock: Cintas agreed 2026-03-10 to buy UniFirst (~$5.5B EV; $155 cash + 0.7720 Cintas shares per share; ~$375M claimed synergies; ~1.5M combined customers). FTC Second Request 2026-06-11; both certified substantial compliance 2026-10-02; timing agreement bars closing before 2026-12-11. Meanwhile Vestis fiscal Q3 2026 revenue -1.8% with pounds processed -4.5%.
incumbents: Cintas, UniFirst, Vestis (Aramark spin-off 2023), Alsco, Elis NA. Route-and-plant model: capture money through weekly rental routes, evergreen contracts, damage/loss charges and price escalators.
incumbent_fragility: The two biggest rivals are merging, so 12-24 months of route consolidation and repricing put a large customer base up for re-bid; Vestis is losing volume and in a $75M cost-cut plan rather than hunting customers; FTC review limits Cintas's aggressiveness before close; asset-heavy laundries and trucks mean they cannot easily go after small accounts profitably; customers dislike auto-renewals and damage charges but have no neutral price benchmark.
funded_startups_already_here: None found attacking US route-based uniform rental (searched uniform/linen startup funding). Adjacent and tiny: bnbkit (Geneva, $1.6M, short-term-rental linen), Quick Smart Wash (India, $5.15M), White Plains Linen (NY, PE-backed by Surge Aug 2025, amount inconsistent, unverified).
wedge_hints: Buyer-side contract audit/exit and re-bid service for SMB renters (auto-renew traps, loss charges, escalators), then a supplier-commissioned marketplace; roll-up/franchise of regional laundries inheriting customers during Cintas/UniFirst route consolidation, especially healthcare and hospitality linen; RFID garment tracking and billing-dispute software for regional operators; any FTC-forced divestiture would be a sudden supply of routes to buy.
insider_roles: Route sales reps and district managers (ex-Cintas/UniFirst), laundry plant GMs and engineers, TRSA member operators, hospital linen/EVS directors, restaurant-group procurement heads, antitrust counsel.

name: US importers' customs-duty payments on industrial inputs and the duty-mitigation services market
size_basis: About $214B of US customs duties over the trailing twelve months through July 2026, from a tracker of Monthly Treasury Statement data (secondary; I did not open the Treasury statement; net monthly figures can dip when duties are refunded). The capturable services fee pool (brokers, counsel, drawback, audits) is a small fraction and was not sized. Overlap flag: finance slice excluded IEEPA refund claims; this pool is duties on Section 232 and 301 goods and the mitigation services.
money_flow: Importers pay duties to CBP, and pay customs brokers, trade counsel and consultants for classification, valuation, origin, drawback and foreign-trade-zone work.
shock: Section 122 surcharge expired 2026-07-24; Section 301 duties (10% or 12.5%) on goods from 60 economies took effect 2026-07-23 with no statutory sunset and a pending court challenge; Section 232 stacks on top; the formal derivative-inclusions process ended 2026-04-06; IEEPA tariffs were struck down 2026-02-20 and the Court of International Trade ordered refunds with interest in early March 2026. Customs bonds, audits and enforcement are rising.
incumbents: Customs brokers (UPS, Expeditors, Livingston and others, from memory), Big Four and trade-law firms, and trade-software vendors (E2open and similar, from memory); a CBP trade-enforcement tool contract lists Altana as incumbent on the government side.
incumbent_fragility: Hourly-billing brokers and counsel are built for stable rules; tariff stacking changes monthly and classification and origin work is manual and error-prone.
funded_startups_already_here: Altana (about $323-337M total raised, $1B valuation July 2024); Tarifflo (YC S26; AuditLive recovers overpaid duty; $500K+ pre-seed); Tariff Sense (Canada, CAD 220k pre-seed Dec 2025); TariffLens AI (launched May 2026); traide AI (Berlin); Flexport is also active (from memory). Many AI classification entrants but little capital outside Altana.
wedge_hints: Post-entry audits and recovery of overpaid Section 232/301 duties on a contingency basis; first-sale-for-export and drawback programs for mid-market manufacturers; metals-content declarations for Section 232 derivatives (the 15%-by-weight carve-out and annex treatment make this a real data task); supplier origin evidence. Legal premise: contingency fees on duty recovery need a licensed customs broker or counsel in the loop; refund eligibility turns on the 180-day protest window and 2026 court orders.
insider_roles: Licensed customs brokers; import compliance managers at mid-size manufacturers; trade counsel; CBP import specialists; drawback specialists.
